chapter: Civil service, Keyhole club and civil rights
title: The integrated Keyhole nightclub opens in 1950 and the police pressure
summary: The Keyhole opened Easter Saturday 1950 as the first fully integrated club in the South; rival white operators tried to get it closed through liquor-hour laws and police.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition

blocks.x: Yeah. And I worked with him. Well, this other Keyhole Nightclub was a fantastic place. It was the first integrated club in the entire South, which you can consider fully integrated. Now, when was this?

No trouble until after we had operated around and I had gotten all of the business in town, the other clubs were suffering. And the white operators got together themselves. They did everything they could to get the policemen to close the place. And, of course, the liquor control laws in those days had gotten to the place where at 12 o'clock at night you'd have to stop operating and stop drinking. But I was able to operate in our club until 2, 3 o'clock in the morning, not serving any drinks and not having any intoxicated beverages on the premises. People had mostly to see the shows. So, finally when the administration changed and we got some real die-hards in there and they didn't agree with the policy of the keyhole and they closed it down. Supposedly they put padlocks on the board. So, we went to Colt with him and I got an injunction against the police department. They couldn't even come on the premises or not even pass in front of the, close to the premises a certain amount of feet. And, when I went to Colt with him it cost about $18,000 plus the business to win the case. When I won the case for the keyhole, I not only integrated the keyhole, I integrated the state of Texas. Judge Sanders, he's dead, passed a decision. He told him, he says, when you police once go out to this man's place, he says, remember that you wear a badge and don't turn shit.
